content: Maternal death, also referred to as maternal mortality or obstetrical death, is defined as the death of a woman during pregnancy or shortly after its termination. According to the United Nations, in the year 2000, the global maternal mortality figure was estimated at 529,000, with less than 1% of these deaths occurring in developed countries. Despite this, the majority of maternal deaths have been medically preventable for decades, as effective treatments to avert such outcomes have been well-established since the 1950s. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines maternal death as the death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of the termination of pregnancy, regardless of the duration or location of the pregnancy, from any cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management, excluding accidental or incidental causes. Maternal deaths are categorized into direct and indirect causes. Direct maternal deaths result from complications of pregnancy, delivery, or their management. Indirect maternal deaths are pregnancy-related deaths in women with preexisting or newly developed health conditions. Deaths unrelated to pregnancy, such as those caused by accidents or incidental factors, are classified as accidental, incidental, or non-obstetrical maternal deaths. Maternal mortality is considered a sentinel event for evaluating the quality of a healthcare system. However, several issues must be acknowledged. The WHO definition is one of many, and other definitions may include accidental and incidental causes. For instance, deaths due to violence against women, which may be influenced by pregnancy and the surrounding socioeconomic and cultural environment, are sometimes included. Additionally, approximately 10% of maternal deaths occur late, meaning after 42 days post-pregnancy termination or delivery. Some definitions extend the observation period to one year after the end of gestation. It is also widely recognized that maternal mortality figures are often significantly underreported. The primary causes of maternal death include bacterial infections, toxemia, obstetrical hemorrhage, ectopic pregnancy, puerperal sepsis, amniotic fluid embolism, and complications from abortions. According to the 2005 WHO report Make Every Mother and Child Count, the leading causes are severe bleeding/hemorrhage (25%), infections (13%), eclampsia (12%), obstructed labor (8%), complications of abortion (13%), other direct causes (8%), and indirect causes (20%). Indirect causes, such as malaria, anemia, HIV/AIDS, and cardiovascular disease, either complicate pregnancy or are exacerbated by it. Complications from hyperemesis gravidarum can also lead to maternal death. The maternal mortality ratio (MMR) is defined as the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births. This ratio is a key indicator of the quality of a healthcare system. In 2000, Sierra Leone had the highest maternal mortality rate at 2,000 deaths per 100,000 live births, followed by Afghanistan at 1,900. In contrast, Iceland had the lowest rate at 0, and Austria reported 4 deaths per 100,000 live births. In the United States, the maternal mortality rate was 17 per 100,000 live births in 2000. The lifetime risk of maternal death accounts for the number of pregnancies and the associated risk. In sub-Saharan Africa, the lifetime risk of maternal death is 1 in 16, compared to 1 in 2,800 in developed nations. A 2003 report by WHO, UNICEF, and UNFPA, based on 2000 data, indicated a global average MMR of 400, with developed regions averaging 20 and developing regions averaging 440. The countries with the worst maternal mortality ratios included Sierra Leone (2,000), Afghanistan (1,900), Malawi (1,800), Angola (1,700), Niger (1,600), Tanzania (1,500), Rwanda (1,400), Mali (1,200), and others such as Somalia, Zimbabwe, Chad, and the Central African Republic (1,100 each). The term maternal mortality rate is often used interchangeably with maternal mortality ratio, but this is a misnomer, as it is technically a ratio, not a rate. High maternal death rates are often observed in countries with high infant mortality rates, reflecting poor nutrition and inadequate medical care. Low birth weight in infants increases the risk of maternal death from cardiovascular disease. For every pound decrease in infant birth weight, the risk of maternal death doubles. Conversely, higher infant birth weights are associated with a lower risk of maternal death. In the 20th century, maternal death rates declined dramatically. At the beginning of the century, maternal death rates were approximately 1 in 100 live births. Today, in the United States, the rate is 13 per 100,000 live births, representing a 100-fold decrease. This decline is largely attributed to advancements in aseptic techniques, the use of cesarean sections, improved fluid management and blood transfusion practices, and better prenatal care.
